title: ARIA roles should suit the element they are on
summary: An element has a role that does not fit its native meaning, such as a heading marked as a button. Use a native element or a suitable role.
problem: A role attribute is set on an element where that role is not recommended, such as role="button" on an <h2>. The role replaces the element's own meaning, so the heading stops being a heading and its keyboard behavior is still missing.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users who jump between headings, links or buttons find the page does not match what they expect. Keyboard users get no built-in behavior, because a role changes what is announced and does not add focus or key handling.
steps: Find the element and its role in the scan result.
If a native element already does the job, use it. A control that acts like a button should be a <button>.
If you need both meanings, nest them: put a <button> inside the heading rather than putting a button role on the heading.
If the role is only there to remove default semantics, check whether the element needs it at all, and take the role off if not.
whyItMatters: This is a best practice, not a WCAG failure. It still helps because mismatched roles hide the real structure of a page, such as its headings, and they tend to ship without keyboard support.
howToCheck: Re-run the scan. In your browser's accessibility inspector, check that the element now reports the role you intended, and that the heading still appears in the page outline.
